title: How do we read angles on a protractor with no numbers?
description: Three angles are read on the book's unlabelled protractor by counting the long marks of ten units and the medium marks of five units, and each count is checked by counting in fives.
teaching_notes: One idea: the long marks come every ten degrees and the medium marks every five, so an angle can be counted in tens or fives. Watch for children who count the long marks as single units.

source: Figure it out (after Unlabelled protractor), Q1
video_script.why: The child reads three angles on the unlabelled protractor by counting in tens and fives, as the book asks.
video_script.substitution: The book's unlabelled protractor, with a long mark at every ten degrees and a medium mark five degrees after each long mark.
video_script.anchor: the book's unlabelled protractor with the vertex A at its centre and the points K, L, W and T on its arms
video_script.payoff_line: Angle K eigh L is thirty degrees. Angle W eigh L is fifty degrees. Angle T eigh K is one hundred and twenty degrees.

final_answer.value: ∠KAL = 30°; ∠WAL = 50°; ∠TAK = 120°; yes, we can count in 5s or 10s
final_answer.spoken: angle K eigh L is thirty degrees, angle W eigh L is fifty degrees, angle T eigh K is one hundred and twenty degrees, and yes, we can count in fives or tens

maths_rules: the vertex A is at the centre of the protractor, so the units of 1 degree between two arms give the angle
a long mark comes at every 10 degrees and a medium mark comes 5 degrees after each long mark
angle KAL: the book counts 30 units, which is 3 long steps, 3 x 10 = 30
check by fives: 6 x 5 = 30, 10 x 5 = 50, 24 x 5 = 120
video_script.design: The unlabelled protractor stays on the board. Long steps are lit teal and medium steps amber. The counts fill in beside each angle as the steps go on.
